messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi Patel had worked as a paramedic in Chicago for more than three decades, and for most of that time he had thought of himself as the kind of man who could stay steady when others could not. That belief changed on a winter evening when he and his partner were called to a warehouse district site after a spill from a damaged industrial container. The air inside the loading bay had a sharp chemical sting, and the first thing Ravi noticed was the smell of alcohol mixed with something metallic and bitter. Within minutes his throat burned, his eyes watered, and several workers began coughing as the corridor filled with darkness from a power failure that made the narrow space feel even smaller. Ravi had later said that what made the scene unbearable was not only the toxicity itself, but the helplessness of being there in his uniform and still not being able to keep everyone safe. The memory of that night now returned to him with startling force whenever he walked past a hospital entrance, heard an ambulance pull up, or even glanced toward a dark hallway at work; sometimes the memory came on without warning from something as ordinary as a passing whiff of alcohol-based sanitizer. When it arrived, he did not experience it as a distant recollection but as a full return of the same terror, his body jolting as if he were back in the warehouse, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing because the emotion became too overwhelming to manage.

In the months after the incident, Ravi found himself spending a great deal of time replaying every decision he had made that night, trying to work out how it could have been prevented. He would lie awake at home after a shift, turning over small details he believed might have changed the outcome, and the rumination gave him a grim sense of control even as it wore him down. That habit of mental review came to structure his days: if he could keep his mind busy with endless analysis, he would not have to sit alone with the memory and the wave of fear that came with it. He also began keeping himself constantly surrounded by people. At home he sought out his wife, children, neighbors, and even casual company from coworkers, and on days off he made sure not to be alone for long. He had come to believe that isolation left him vulnerable to being ambushed by the memory, and being with others gave him a kind of cover, even if he did not talk about what was happening. Yet the more he tried to manage the experience by filling every hour, the more the memory seemed to break through when he least expected it. A smell in a supermarket aisle, the dimness of the garage at dusk, or a glimpse of medical equipment could suddenly pull the full event back into the room, and each intrusion left him more determined to avoid places that reminded him of that night.

Ravi’s efforts to shut out the reminders gradually narrowed his world. He began avoiding hospitals except when absolutely necessary, took longer routes to stay away from ambulance bays, and started delaying routine physical examinations because the exam room, the white walls, and the sound of medical staff moving in the corridor all felt too close to the scene of the spill. At work this became harder to manage. As a paramedic he could not completely escape the settings that now unsettled him, but he became vigilant about where he stood, how dark a hallway looked, and whether an alcohol smell lingered in a room after cleaning. That constant monitoring kept him on edge, and the very things he scanned for—workplace hazards, dark spaces, the sharp scent of alcohol—were the same cues that brought the memory rushing back. Once the memory surged, it strengthened his need to avoid even more, and he would redouble his efforts to stay busy, stay in company, and keep away from medical environments. In turn, those strategies made the reminders feel more immediate: the less he allowed himself to enter a hospital or sit quietly alone, the more foreign and threatening those places became, and the more power they seemed to have when he could not avoid them.

By the time he came for help, Ravi was exhausted by the strain of living this way. He still functioned, but only by arranging his life around avoidance, constant contact with other people, and repeated mental revisiting of the spill, and he felt increasingly ashamed that his work as a paramedic now carried him into the very settings he feared most. What brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep tightening the circle around himself without losing more of his life and his marriage. He was most afraid that one unexpected smell, one dark corridor, or one routine examination would open the memory again and leave him flooded with the same terror in front of other people. At the same time, he was hoping that treatment might help him bear the memory without having to outrun it, and that he could return to work without feeling that every hospital doorway was waiting to pull him back into that warehouse.
